title: Asymmetric rollout: GPU velocity and KV fragmentation playbook
content:
Purpose and context:
This is a pragmatic, simulation-driven playbook to evaluate and mitigate capacity risk when we roll out a new model with larger KV entries and uneven regional demand. Focus is on two coupled failure modes: (1) GPU slot exhaustion from request velocity spikes, and (2) elevated KV cache fragmentation leading to eviction churn that amplifies request latency.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- New model delta: average per-request KV footprint increases from ~48KB to ~320KB (longer contexts + denser token metadata).
- If rolled symmetrically across regions, model admits ~3x more KV per qps; asymmetric rollout (higher weight to US-WEST) can concentrate eviction pressure and cause cascading cold misses in other regions via routing fallbacks.
- Recommended immediate controls: limit ingress velocity per region, pre-seed hot prefixes in high-weight regions, enable conservative co-location (reserve 12% GPU headroom per host pool), and short-term admission control on tail latency thresholds.

Assumptions used in sims (document these in any PR):
- Baseline live model (v1): per-request KV = 48KB, average seq_len = 256, KV hit rate = 0.84 under current cache policy.
- New model (v2): per-request KV = 320KB (median), seq_len = 1024 for 20% of requests, KV hit rate naive = 0.62 without pre-warming.
- Fleet: 1200 GPUs globally, region map: US-WEST (40%), US-EAST (30%), EU (20%), APAC (10%).
- Typical active contexts per GPU = 3.6 when healthy; soft limit target for low-latency ops is 4.5 active contexts.
- KV cache per GPU pool is partitioned with 2:1 user-data:system-data memory split; usable user KV memory per GPU = 24 GB.

Core formulas we used (put in sheet for easy parameter swaps):
- Effective KV memory per qps = qps * average_kv_size * (avg_tokens_per_request / model_chunk_size). (Simplified to qps * avg_kv_size for short-run risk.)
- Eviction burnout threshold = usable_kv_memory / average_kv_size.
- Churn amplification factor (CAF) ~ 1 + eviction_rate * fallthrough_penalty, where fallthrough_penalty approximates extra KV load from fallbacks and re-requests.

Example scenario outputs (high-level):
- Scenario A (aggressive, no prewarm): rollout weight US-WEST 60% -> US-WEST eviction burnout in ~18 hours at projected qps=14k global (US-WEST qps 8.4k). Median latency spike x4, 95p latency x7.
- Scenario B (staggered + seeded): staged 10% -> 30% -> 60% over 7 days with seeded prefixes and shadowing; US-WEST burnout avoided, KV hit rate improves to 0.78 within 48h of seeding.
- Scenario C (asymmetric + admission): same weight as A but with 12% GPU reserve + admission throttle at 1% tail-latency breach -> burnout delayed beyond 72h and graceful degradation path triggers model fallback to v1 for 10% of traffic.

Simulated spreadsheet excerpt (paste into sheet):
| Region   | Fleet % | qps (proj) | Avg KV (KB) | KV mem req (GB/hr) | Burnout hours | Notes |
| US-WEST  | 40%     | 8400       | 320         | 8.6                | 18            | hotspot w/o seed |
| US-EAST  | 30%     | 4200       | 320         | 4.3                | 42            | slower pressure |
| EU       | 20%     | 2800       | 320         | 2.9                | 60            | network fallback risk |
| APAC     | 10%     | 1400       | 320         | 1.4                | 120           | low immediate risk |

Operational playbook (step-by-step):
1) Pre-launch (2–7 days before traffic ramp)
   - Run a prewarm job that injects synthetic prefixes covering top-1k active contexts per region; reuse existing shadowing infra GH-ralph/prewarm-sim.
   - Allocate a transient 'seeding' pool of 6% of GPUs in the high-weight region (US-WEST) and set sticky routing for seeded contexts.

2) Early ramp (day 0–3)
   - Start with 10% traffic. Enforce per-region ingress caps: US-WEST cap = max(2.5k qps) initially.
   - Enable admission control based on 95p token-latency; if breached for >5m, cut rollout rate by 50%.
   - Monitor KV evictions/min and eviction churn ratio. Trigger immediate rollback if churn ratio > 0.25 and tail latency doubling.

3) Mid ramp (day 4–10)
   - Gradually increase to 30–60% based on observed hit rate improvements. Continue prewarming for newly observed hot prefixes.
   - Shift seeded pools from transient to durable if hit rate stays >0.7 for 48h.

4) Full launch
   - If burnout thresholds are not crossed and latency stable, expand route weights to target distribution. Keep 12% fleet reserve for 72h post-full launch.

Mitigations and engineering tasks (owners in parens):
- Implement per-region admission throttle gate with auto rollback (Leah)
- Short-lived seeded pool orchestration and tag-based routing (Arjun)
- KV memory accounting dashboard: eviction heatmap + churn estimator (Owen)
- Quick fallback flag in router to fallback to v1 model for user-subset when tail-latency > threshold (runtime team)
- Small quantized variant test in canary (applied-ml) to reduce average KV by ~30% — track quality delta.

Questions & open decisions:
- How long should seeded pool be retained before being absorbed into main fleet? (current default suggestion: 48h stable >0.7 hit rate)
- Should we prioritize region-specific quantized variants (i.e., APAC uses q3 variant) vs unified model? Cost/ops trade-off pending.

Quick checklist to attach to rollout ticket INFRA-8421:
- [ ] Prewarm job scheduled and passed (smoke)
- [ ] Admission throttle implemented and can be overridden manually
- [ ] Dashboard panels created and shared with SRE on-call
- [ ] Run a dry-run with 0.5% real traffic for 6 hours to validate hit-rate uplift

Notes, rough math, and scratch space: (capture intermediate numbers)
- usable_kv_per_gpu = 24GB -> 24*1024 = 24576 MB -> 25165824 KB. At avg_kv=320KB -> ~78k active entries per GPU if only this model; but actual churn + multi-model means safe occupancy is ~12–16k entries (hence reserve).
- With qps=8400 in US-WEST, and avg request rate 0.33s per request concurrency, active contexts per GPU skyrockets if we co-locate too many hot prefixes.

Appendix: raw simulation knobs (put in sheet cells)
- avg_kv_size_kb, per_region_qps, seed_pool_pct, initial_rollout_pct, admission_latency_threshold_ms, reserve_gpu_pct, fallback_traffic_pct

Bottom line: this is a conservative, observable-first rollout pattern that accepts a small pacing delay in exchange for avoiding nonlinear cascading failures from KV fragmentation. Use this as the canonical plan for any model whose per-request KV footprint increases >4x relative to baseline.
